LESSON: WRITING 3.3.1 WRITING FOR INFORMATION – PARAGRAPHS

Grade: Grade 8
Subject: INDIGENOUS LANGUAGES
Strand: Strand 3
Topic 3.3: Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs

SECTION 1: WELCOME

Hello! This is a study lesson on Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs. Read the explanation, follow every worked example, then do the practice. This is original CBC Learn content written from KICD outcomes — not a copy of a commercial textbook.

Big question: How do we write paragraphs?

SECTION 2: WHAT YOU WILL LEARN

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. identify the features of a well-developed paragraph
2. compose two well sequenced paragraphs on the theme for information

SECTION 3: STUDY NOTES (READ AND LEARN)

WHAT YOU ARE STUDYING: WRITING 3.3.1 WRITING FOR INFORMATION – PARAGRAPHS
Subject: INDIGENOUS LANGUAGES · Grade: Grade 8
This is a learner study lesson (not a teacher guide). Read every part, follow the models, then practise.

BIG PICTURE
Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs helps you succeed in INDIGENOUS LANGUAGES. You will understand it, practise it, and use it at school, at home, and in your community in Kenya.

KEY FACTS: WRITING 3.3.1 WRITING FOR INFORMATION – PARAGRAPHS
Language skills grow by daily practice: listen carefully, speak clearly, read every day, write neatly.
Model → guided practice → independent practice.
Always use complete sentences when writing answers.

PART 1: Identify the features of a well-developed paragraph

What this means
In this part you learn to identify the features of a well-developed paragraph. You will use ideas from at school, at home, and in your community in Kenya.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: identify the features of a well-developed paragraph.
2. Listen, speak, read, then write using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Model reading: Read a short paragraph about “Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs”, then retell it in 3 sentences.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can identify the features of a well-developed paragraph. Write or say your answer clearly.

PART 2: Compose two well sequenced paragraphs on the theme for information

What this means
In this part you learn to compose two well sequenced paragraphs on the theme for information. You will use ideas from at school, at home, and in your community in Kenya.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: compose two well sequenced paragraphs on the theme for information.
2. Listen, speak, read, then write using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Model speaking: Say 4 clear sentences about Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs to a partner.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can compose two well sequenced paragraphs on the theme for information. Write or say your answer clearly.

PUT IT TOGETHER
Close your notes and say aloud: what Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs is, one example, and one way you will practise this week.

SECTION 4: QUICK EXAMPLES

Example 1: Read a short paragraph about “Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs”, then retell it in 3 sentences. (skill: identify the features of a well-developed paragraph)

Example 2: Say 4 clear sentences about Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs to a partner. (skill: compose two well sequenced paragraphs on the theme for information)

SECTION 5: PRACTICE NOW

1. Write 5 sentences (or show 5 clear steps) that teach Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs to a classmate.
2. Practise this skill: identify the features of a well-developed paragraph.
3. Practise this skill: compose two well sequenced paragraphs on the theme for information.
4. Make one local Kenya example of Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs from your county, market, farm, or school.
5. Mark your own work: What did you get right? What will you redo?

SECTION 6: WORK TO DO (HOME / REVISION)

1. In your exercise book, make a one-page revision sheet for Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs: meaning, 3 examples, 5 practice items.
2. Teach a parent/guardian or younger sibling one part of this lesson (2 minutes).
3. Answer in writing: Why should a Grade 8 learner study Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs?
4. Prepare for the quiz: cover the Remember box and recite it.

SECTION: THINK ABOUT IT

1. How do we write paragraphs?
2. Why is it important to preserve wildlife?

SECTION: REMEMBER

1. Know what Writing 3.3.1 Writing for information – Paragraphs means in your own words.
2. Use local Kenyan examples, not only definitions.
3. Practise in small steps, then check your work.
4. Be able to: identify the features of a well-developed paragraph.
5. Be able to: compose two well sequenced paragraphs on the theme for information.

Now complete the Revision Quiz. Open Answers only after you finish.

— CBC Learn · Original study notes from KICD outcomes (Strategy 2)
